title: Compute, Storage, and Networking
tagline: The three pillars of cloud infrastructure — understanding VMs, storage types, and virtual networks is the vocabulary of every architecture diagram.

sections.content:
Every cloud workload, regardless of size or complexity, ultimately reduces to three concerns: **compute** (something to run your code), **storage** (somewhere to persist your data), and **networking** (a way to move data between components, users, and services). Before cloud computing, each of these required physical hardware that you bought, racked, and maintained yourself. Today, all three are available on-demand as software-defined resources, billed by the hour or even the millisecond. Understanding how they work, why they are designed the way they are, and how to pick the right option for a given workload is the core vocabulary of cloud engineering.

The three pillars are deeply intertwined. A compute instance cannot function without storage for its operating system. A web application cannot serve users without networking. A distributed database requires all three simultaneously and must carefully coordinate access across them. Getting the combination right is the difference between a resilient, cost-effective architecture and one that is slow, expensive, or fragile — problems that typically only surface months into production when data volumes and traffic spike beyond early estimates.

Cloud providers — AWS, Google Cloud, Azure — expose compute primarily as **virtual machines** and **containers**, storage as **object, block, or file systems**, and networking as **Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs)** complete with subnets, routing tables, security groups, NAT gateways, and load balancers. Each abstraction hides enormous engineering complexity behind a clean API. Behind a single `aws ec2 run-instances` call is a hypervisor scheduling CPU time, a distributed storage network backing your root disk, and a software-defined switch enforcing your firewall rules — all invisible to you.

This chapter builds a deep, working understanding of each pillar: what it is, how the underlying mechanism works, why each design choice was made, when to choose which option, and the most common mistakes engineers make. By the end you will be able to read an AWS architecture diagram and understand not just what each component is named but why it is placed where it is.

sections.title: The Corporate Office Campus
sections.content:
Picture a large corporate campus with several buildings, each serving a different function. **Virtual machines** are private offices — each employee (workload) gets a dedicated room with their own desk, filing cabinet, and door lock, even though the building itself is shared with others. You pay for the room whether you are using it or not. **Containers** are hot-desk co-working spaces on a shared floor — faster to set up, cheaper, you bring only what you need for the day, but you share the elevator shaft (the host OS kernel) with everyone else on the floor.

**Object storage** is the corporate archive room in the basement — vast, climate-controlled, and you can store any document, but you access it by submitting a retrieval request with the document's reference number (an HTTP GET with the object key), not by browsing the shelves yourself at random. You cannot change a page in an archived document — you check it out, modify it, and file a new version. **Block storage** is the filing cabinet bolted to the desk in your private office — fast, your own, great for documents you need to edit constantly (database files), but only your machine has the key. **File storage** is a shared network drive mounted by everyone in the building — great for shared documents, but slower and pricier than the personal cabinet.

**The VPC** is the campus perimeter fence and badge-access system. **Public subnets** are the lobby and visitor areas — anyone off the street can walk in (reach your public IP). **Private subnets** are secured inner floors — only badge-holders can enter (only internal traffic can reach those instances). **Security groups** are the individual room access rules — Marketing can enter Room 80 and 443, but only IT can enter the server room on port 5432. **The load balancer** is the receptionist who routes visitors to whichever available team member can help, automatically skipping anyone who has called in sick (a failed health check).

sections.title: Compute: Virtual Machines — The Foundation
sections.content:
A **virtual machine (VM)** is an emulated computer running inside a real computer. The physical server (the **host**) runs a piece of software called a **hypervisor** — either bare-metal (Type 1, like AWS Nitro, VMware ESXi, or KVM) or hosted on top of an OS (Type 2, like VirtualBox). The hypervisor intercepts hardware instructions from the guest OS and either executes them directly on the CPU (using hardware virtualization extensions like Intel VT-x or AMD-V) or translates them — giving the illusion of dedicated hardware.

From the guest OS's perspective, it owns the CPUs, RAM, and disk it was allocated. In reality, the hypervisor is multiplexing dozens or hundreds of VMs onto one large physical server. AWS Nitro — Amazon's custom hypervisor — offloads networking and storage I/O entirely to dedicated hardware ASICs, freeing nearly all CPU and memory for the guest, which is why cloud VMs can approach bare-metal performance for many workloads.

Each VM runs its own complete operating system — kernel, drivers, system libraries. This isolation is the VM's great strength: a kernel panic in one VM cannot crash another. It is also the VM's cost: booting a full OS takes minutes, and each VM consumes hundreds of megabytes of RAM just for its OS overhead.

**Instance families** on AWS reflect different hardware profiles:
- `t3`/`t4g` — burstable general-purpose; CPU credits accumulate during idle time and are spent during bursts. Perfect for development, light web servers, and variable workloads.
- `c6i`/`c7g` — compute-optimized; high CPU-to-RAM ratio; ideal for CPU-bound workloads like video encoding, scientific computing, and game servers.
- `r6i`/`r7g` — memory-optimized; high RAM-to-CPU ratio; for in-memory databases (Redis clusters), real-time analytics, and large JVM heaps.
- `p3`/`p4d` — GPU instances with NVIDIA V100 or A100 GPUs; machine learning training and inference, graphics rendering.
- `i3`/`i4i` — storage-optimized; NVMe SSDs directly attached, not network-attached; for high-throughput databases like Cassandra.

**Right-sizing** matters enormously for cost. An over-provisioned `r5.4xlarge` for a workload that would fit on an `r5.xlarge` wastes four times the money. Cloud providers offer tools like AWS Compute Optimizer that analyze CloudWatch metrics and recommend downsizing or family changes.

sections.title: Compute: Containers — Lighter, Faster, More Portable
sections.content:
**Containers** solve a different problem than VMs. Rather than isolating at the hardware level, they isolate at the **process level** using two Linux kernel features: **namespaces** (which give a process its own view of the filesystem, network stack, process tree, user IDs, and hostname) and **cgroups** (which limit the CPU, memory, and I/O that a process group can consume).

Because containers share the host OS kernel, they have almost no boot overhead — a container starts in milliseconds. They also carry no per-container OS weight: a minimal Node.js container image might be 100 MB versus 1–2 GB for a full VM snapshot. This density advantage means you can pack ten times as many containers onto a host as VMs, which is why container-based deployment dramatically reduces compute costs for stateless services.

The trade-off is isolation depth. A kernel vulnerability in the host OS can affect all containers on that host; a kernel bug cannot easily escape a VM's hypervisor boundary (though VM escape vulnerabilities exist, they are rare and high-severity). For this reason, security-sensitive multi-tenant workloads often use VMs, while same-trust microservices within one team use containers.

**Docker** is the dominant container runtime and image format. A `Dockerfile` describes how to build an image — layered filesystem snapshots. **Kubernetes** (K8s) is the de-facto orchestrator: it schedules containers onto a fleet of nodes, handles rolling deployments, scales based on CPU/memory metrics (HPA), and restarts crashed containers. Managed Kubernetes offerings — **EKS** (AWS), **GKE** (Google), **AKS** (Azure) — handle the control plane, so you only manage worker nodes.

Containers are **stateless by design** — when a container restarts, its filesystem changes are lost (unless mounted to a persistent volume). Persistent data lives in external storage: databases use managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL) or block volumes mounted as Kubernetes PersistentVolumes; binary assets go to object storage. This separation of stateless compute from stateful storage is a core cloud-native design principle.

sections.title: Storage: Object Storage — The Infinite Filing Room
sections.content:
**Object storage** (S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage) stores arbitrary binary data — files, images, videos, backups, ML datasets, log archives — as **objects** in flat **buckets**. Each object is identified by a globally unique **key** (a string like `users/avatars/user-1234.jpg`) and retrieved via HTTP GET/PUT operations through a REST API.

The internal architecture of object storage is radically different from a filesystem. There are no directories — the key is just a string; the `/` in a key is a naming convention that tools simulate as folders, but the storage layer sees only key-value pairs. Objects are not modified in-place; you always upload a complete new version (though versioning features allow you to keep history). There are no locks, no atomic multi-object updates, and until recently no strong read-after-write consistency across objects (S3 gained strong consistency in December 2020).

What makes object storage special is its **scale and durability**. S3 achieves **99.999999999% (11 nines)** durability by storing each object redundantly across multiple Availability Zones — physically separate data centers. Lose one entire AZ to a fire or flood and your data is safe. Capacity is effectively unlimited; S3 stores exabytes of data across its entire fleet. And the price is extraordinary: roughly **$0.023/GB-month** for S3 Standard — roughly three times cheaper than block storage.

Object storage is accessed **over the network** with higher latency (typically 5–50ms per request, depending on object size and region) than block storage. This makes it unsuitable for database files, which need sub-millisecond random reads, but ideal for web assets, backups, and data lake storage where you read large files sequentially. Combined with a CDN like **CloudFront**, object storage serves static content (JavaScript bundles, images, videos) to users globally with low latency, since the CDN caches objects at edge locations near users.

**Storage classes** let you trade access speed for cost: S3 Standard → S3 Standard-IA (infrequent access, cheaper but per-retrieval cost) → S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval → S3 Glacier Deep Archive (~$0.00099/GB-month, retrieval in hours). **Lifecycle policies** can automatically move objects between classes as they age — e.g., move logs to Glacier after 30 days.

sections.title: Storage: Block Storage — The Fast Local Disk
sections.content:
**Block storage** (EBS on AWS, Persistent Disk on GCP, Azure Managed Disks) presents to a VM exactly like a physical hard drive: a fixed-size sequence of fixed-size blocks (512 bytes or 4 KB), readable and writable at arbitrary offsets. The OS formats it with a filesystem (ext4, NTFS, XFS), mounts it, and reads/writes files through the VFS layer just as if it were a local disk.

Behind the scenes, EBS is not physically attached to your EC2 instance — it is a **network-attached virtual disk** served from a distributed storage system over a dedicated, high-throughput internal network (separate from the data-plane network your application uses). AWS Nitro moves EBS I/O to a dedicated hardware card, giving up to **64,000 IOPS** (for `io2 Block Express`) with sub-millisecond latency — close to the performance of a local NVMe SSD.

Volume types reflect different performance-cost tradeoffs:
- `gp3` (general purpose SSD) — **baseline: 3,000 IOPS, 125 MB/s throughput**, independently configurable up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s. The default for most workloads. ~$0.08/GB-month.
- `io2`/`io2 Block Express` — provisioned IOPS SSD for **I/O-intensive databases** needing consistent sub-millisecond latency; up to 256,000 IOPS on Block Express. Significantly more expensive.
- `st1` — HDD-backed throughput-optimized storage for **big sequential reads**: data warehouses, log processing. Cheap per GB, but high latency for random I/O.
- `sc1` — cold HDD, the cheapest EBS option; for infrequently accessed sequential workloads.

The critical architectural constraint: **EBS volumes are scoped to a single Availability Zone**. A volume in `us-east-1a` cannot be mounted by an instance in `us-east-1b`. To move data across AZs, you must create a **snapshot** (a point-in-time copy stored in S3), then restore from that snapshot in the target AZ. This is why database high-availability solutions use managed services like **RDS Multi-AZ**, which maintains synchronous standby replicas in a different AZ rather than trying to share a block volume.

Another critical constraint: **a standard EBS volume can be attached to only one EC2 instance at a time** (though `io1`/`io2` support multi-attach for clustered filesystems that handle their own locking, a specialized use case). If you need shared filesystem access across multiple instances, you need file storage.

sections.title: Storage: File Storage — The Shared Network Drive
sections.content:
**File storage** (AWS EFS, Google Filestore, Azure Files) provides a fully managed **POSIX-compatible network filesystem** that can be mounted simultaneously by hundreds or thousands of compute instances. From the application's perspective it looks and behaves exactly like a local directory — `open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `rename()` all work as expected — but under the hood traffic flows over NFS (Network File System) or SMB.

File storage fills a specific gap: legacy enterprise applications and some modern workloads (content management systems like WordPress, shared ML training checkpoints, home directories for HPC clusters) were written to expect a POSIX filesystem and cannot easily be refactored to use object storage's HTTP API. EFS lets you lift-and-shift these workloads without code changes.

The trade-offs are real. EFS Standard costs approximately **$0.30/GB-month** — about 13x more expensive than S3 Standard and 4x more than EBS gp3 per GB. Latency is also higher than block storage because every I/O traverses the network twice (client to NFS server, NFS server to underlying block storage). For latency-sensitive or high-IOPS workloads, EFS is the wrong choice.

For most greenfield cloud-native applications, the decision tree is simple: object storage for blobs and files you access by key; block storage for databases and OS volumes where you need random I/O performance; file storage only when you need POSIX semantics shared across multiple instances and cannot rewrite the application.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── COMPUTE: inspect running EC2 instances ──────────────────────────────────
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name,Placement.AvailabilityZone]' \
  --output table --region us-east-1

# Launch a t3.micro instance into a private subnet with a security group
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abc123private \
  --security-group-ids sg-0webservers \
  --count 1 \
  --no-associate-public-ip-address

# ── STORAGE: Object Storage (S3) ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Create a bucket and upload a file
aws s3 mb s3://my-app-assets-20240101 --region us-east-1
aws s3 cp ./dist/bundle.js s3://my-app-assets-20240101/static/bundle.js

# Sync an entire directory (incremental upload)
aws s3 sync ./dist/ s3://my-app-assets-20240101/static/ --delete

# Generate a pre-signed URL (time-limited access without making bucket public)
aws s3 presign s3://my-app-assets-20240101/private/report.pdf --expires-in 3600

# ── STORAGE: Block Storage (EBS) ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Create a 100 GB gp3 volume in us-east-1a with 6000 IOPS
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --size 100 \
  --volume-type gp3 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a \
  --iops 6000 \
  --throughput 250

# Create a snapshot for cross-AZ migration or backup
aws ec2 create-snapshot \
  --volume-id vol-0abc123 \
  --description "Pre-deploy snapshot $(date +%Y%m%d)"

# ── NETWORKING: VPC and Security Groups ─────────────────────────────────────
# Create a security group for web servers
aws ec2 create-security-group \
  --group-name web-sg \
  --description "Web tier: HTTPS from internet" \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123

# Allow HTTPS from internet; Postgres only from the web security group
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-web --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-db  --protocol tcp --port 5432 \
  --source-group sg-web  # only instances in sg-web can reach the database
sections.explanation: The security group source-group rule (`--source-group sg-web`) is more robust than an IP CIDR rule: as EC2 instances scale in and out, new instances automatically inherit their group membership, so the database rule applies without any IP management. The pre-signed URL pattern lets you serve private S3 objects to authenticated users without making the bucket public — a common pattern for downloadable invoices, reports, and user-uploaded files.

sections.title: Networking: Virtual Private Cloud — Your Isolated Network
sections.content:
A **Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)** is a logically isolated section of a cloud provider's network that you define and control. It is software-defined networking: routers, switches, firewalls, and NAT gateways are all running as software on the provider's physical infrastructure, but they behave from your perspective exactly like dedicated hardware you own.

When you create a VPC, you assign it a **CIDR block** — a range of private IP addresses (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16` gives you 65,536 addresses from `10.0.0.0` to `10.0.255.255`). You carve this range into **subnets**, each associated with one Availability Zone. A `/24` subnet (e.g., `10.0.1.0/24`) provides 256 addresses, with 5 reserved by AWS for routing, broadcasting, and internal DNS.

**The internet gateway / route table distinction** is fundamental. A subnet is **public** if its route table has a route sending `0.0.0.0/0` traffic to an **Internet Gateway (IGW)**. A subnet is **private** if its default route sends internet-bound traffic to a **NAT Gateway** (or has no route at all). Instances in a public subnet can have public IP addresses and receive inbound traffic from the internet. Instances in a private subnet cannot receive inbound internet traffic under any circumstances — even if you misconfigure a security group to allow it, there is simply no network path. This is the correct defense-in-depth posture for databases and internal services.

For private instances that need to download software or reach external APIs (outbound internet), a **NAT Gateway** in the public subnet allows outbound connections while keeping the private instance unreachable from outside. The NAT Gateway has a public IP and translates outbound traffic from private instances, but does not forward unsolicited inbound connections back to them.

**VPC Peering** connects two VPCs (in the same or different accounts/regions) so their instances can communicate using private IP addresses without traversing the internet. **AWS PrivateLink** lets you expose a service from one VPC to another through an endpoint, without peering the entire networks. **Transit Gateway** acts as a regional hub, connecting many VPCs and on-premise networks through one managed router — the enterprise-grade alternative to the complex mesh of VPC peering connections that becomes unmanageable at scale.

sections.title: Networking: Security Groups and Network ACLs
sections.content:
Cloud networking provides two layers of traffic filtering that are often confused.

**Security Groups** are **stateful** virtual firewalls attached to individual **network interfaces** (i.e., specific EC2 instances or RDS databases). Stateful means: if you create an inbound rule allowing TCP on port 443, the corresponding outbound response traffic is automatically allowed without needing an explicit outbound rule. Security groups are **deny by default** — all inbound traffic is blocked unless explicitly permitted. You can reference other security groups as a source (e.g., "allow port 5432 from sg-web"), which is cleaner than IP ranges because it updates automatically as instances join or leave the group.

**Network ACLs (NACLs)** are **stateless** firewalls attached to entire **subnets**. Stateless means: you must explicitly allow both inbound and outbound traffic for a connection. NACLs evaluate rules in numbered order (100, 200, 300…) and stop at the first match. They are a coarser tool — typically used for subnet-wide blocks (e.g., denying traffic from a known malicious IP range) rather than instance-level policy. For most architectures, security groups provide sufficient control and NACLs add operational complexity without proportional benefit.

The **principle of least privilege** is the guiding rule: allow only the minimum required traffic from the minimum required sources on the minimum required ports. Common patterns:
- Public-facing load balancer: allow TCP 80 and 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`; allow nothing else inbound.
- Application servers: allow traffic only from the load balancer's security group, not from the open internet.
- Database: allow the database port (5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL) only from the application servers' security group.
- All outbound: allow all outbound from app servers (they need to reach S3, external APIs, etc.) but restrict database outbound to only what is needed.

sections.title: Networking: Load Balancers — Distributing Traffic for Scale and Resilience
sections.content:
A **load balancer** sits in front of a fleet of compute instances and distributes incoming requests across them. This achieves two things simultaneously: **horizontal scale** (more traffic handled by adding more instances) and **high availability** (if one instance fails its health check, the load balancer stops routing to it within seconds).

AWS provides three types, reflecting different layers of the OSI model:

**Application Load Balancer (ALB)** operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). It terminates TLS, decrypts the request, inspects HTTP headers, URL path, hostname, and query parameters, and makes routing decisions based on rules. This enables powerful patterns:
- **Path-based routing**: `/api/*` → backend microservice; `/*` → React SPA; `/images/*` → S3 bucket.
- **Host-based routing**: `api.example.com` → API service; `admin.example.com` → admin service — all behind one ALB.
- **Weighted target groups**: send 10% of traffic to a new canary version, 90% to the stable version — for blue/green deployments.
- **User authentication**: ALB integrates with Cognito or OIDC to require login before routing requests, offloading auth from the application.

**Network Load Balancer (NLB)** operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). It does not inspect HTTP content — it simply forwards packets to a target based on port and IP. NLB is designed for **ultra-low latency** (sub-millisecond) and **very high throughput** (millions of connections per second). Use it for non-HTTP protocols (database proxies, MQTT, gaming servers, financial data feeds) or when the application requires static Elastic IPs for allowlisting.

**Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)** is a specialized type for routing traffic through third-party network appliances (firewalls, intrusion detection systems) transparently. It operates at Layer 3.

**Health checks** are how the load balancer detects failures. For an ALB, it sends HTTP requests to each target on a configured path (e.g., `GET /health`) every 30 seconds (configurable) and expects a 2xx response within a timeout. After a configurable number of consecutive failures (unhealthyThresholdCount, default 2), the target is marked unhealthy and removed from rotation. This means an application crash is detected within 60 seconds and traffic automatically fails over to healthy instances — without human intervention.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The ALB is placed in two public subnets across different AZs for high availability — if one AZ loses power, the ALB in the other AZ continues serving traffic. The path rule (priority 100) intercepts `/api/*` before the default rule, routing it to the backend. Health checks with unhealthyThresholdCount=2 and interval=30s mean a crashed container is removed from rotation within 60 seconds.

sections.title: Putting It Together: How the Three Pillars Interact
sections.content:
Understanding each pillar in isolation is necessary but not sufficient. Real systems require careful thinking about how they interact, especially around **failure modes** and **latency boundaries**.

Consider a web application with these components: an ALB distributing traffic to two EC2 instances in private subnets across two AZs, each instance with a mounted EBS volume for temporary work, a PostgreSQL RDS instance (Multi-AZ), and S3 for storing user uploads. What happens when:

**An AZ goes down**: The ALB health checks detect the instance in the failed AZ and removes it. RDS fails over automatically to the standby replica in the healthy AZ (typically 60–120 seconds of downtime during the failover). S3 data is safe — it replicates across multiple AZs by design. The EBS volume in the failed AZ is unavailable, but because the instances used it only for temporary scratch space (not the database), no data is lost.

**Traffic spikes 10x**: The ALB distributes load across the healthy instances. With **Auto Scaling**, the EC2 fleet can launch new instances within 2–5 minutes (time to provision, configure, and pass health checks) and register them with the ALB automatically. RDS may become the bottleneck — **read replicas** can absorb some read load, and **ElastiCache** (Redis) can cache frequent queries in memory, reducing database I/O.

**A developer accidentally deletes a critical S3 object**: With **S3 Versioning** enabled, deleted objects are only soft-deleted (a delete marker is added). The previous version can be restored. Without versioning, the object is gone. For RDS, **automated backups** and **point-in-time recovery** let you restore to any second within the backup retention window (up to 35 days).

This failure-mode analysis is the core of **Well-Architected** design — understanding not just the happy path but what happens when each component fails, and ensuring that single-component failures do not cause total system outages.

**A brief history of cloud infrastructure abstractions**: AWS launched EC2 (virtual machines) in 2006 and S3 (object storage) the same year — two of the first cloud services ever offered commercially. VPCs were added in 2009 to give customers network isolation; before that, EC2 instances ran in a shared flat network (EC2-Classic) where any instance could potentially talk to any other. The Nitro hypervisor arrived in 2017 and fundamentally changed EC2 performance by offloading I/O to dedicated hardware, allowing VMs to approach bare-metal speeds. Containers reached the mainstream with Docker in 2013; AWS launched ECS in 2014 and EKS (managed Kubernetes) in 2018. This history explains why older AWS accounts may still have resources in EC2-Classic and why older architectures often look nothing like modern VPC-based designs.

**Common architectural mistakes and interview traps**:
- **Putting databases in public subnets** — never do this. Even with a security group, a public subnet has a route to the internet. Private subnets are the correct defense-in-depth.
- **Using object storage for database files** — object storage has 5–50ms latency per request. A database performing thousands of random I/Os per second would be catastrophically slow. Use block storage (EBS) for databases.
- **Ignoring AZ scoping of EBS volumes** — an EBS volume in `us-east-1a` cannot attach to an instance in `us-east-1b`. This is a frequent source of failed failovers. Use Multi-AZ RDS or Aurora instead of manually managed EBS-attached databases.
- **ALB vs NLB confusion**: ALB for HTTP/HTTPS (Layer 7, content-aware routing); NLB for raw TCP/UDP (Layer 4, ultra-low latency). Both perform health checks and distribute traffic — they differ in inspection depth and protocol support.
- **Security group vs NACL**: security groups are stateful (response traffic auto-allowed) and instance-scoped; NACLs are stateless (must allow both directions) and subnet-scoped. In interviews, if asked 'what is stateful about security groups' — the key word is the return traffic rule is implicit.

items: **Virtual machines** virtualize hardware via a hypervisor, running a full guest OS per instance — strong isolation, minutes to boot, high per-instance RAM overhead. Choose instance families by workload: `t`-series for burstable general-purpose, `c`-series for CPU-intensive, `r`-series for memory-intensive, `p`-series for GPU/ML.

**Containers** share the host OS kernel via Linux namespaces and cgroups — millisecond startup, no OS overhead, 10x denser than VMs, but shallower isolation. Stateless by design; persistent data lives in external storage (managed databases or EBS volumes mounted as K8s PersistentVolumes).

**Object storage** (S3) is the cheapest (~$0.023/GB-month), most durable (11 nines), and most scalable storage option — ideal for blobs, backups, assets, and data lakes. Access is via HTTP GET/PUT (not POSIX); latency is 5–50ms, making it unsuitable for database random I/O.

**Block storage** (EBS) behaves like a local disk — low-latency random IOPS for databases and OS volumes. Zone-scoped (an EBS volume in AZ-a cannot attach to an instance in AZ-b). Use `gp3` for general workloads, `io2` for high-IOPS databases. Snapshots enable cross-AZ copies.

**File storage** (EFS) provides POSIX-compatible shared NFS storage mountable by many instances simultaneously — use only when legacy apps require it or when multiple instances need shared write access to a filesystem. ~13x more expensive than S3 per GB.

**VPCs** are isolated virtual networks you define; public subnets route internet-bound traffic through an Internet Gateway; private subnets route outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway but have no inbound internet path — always place databases and internal services in private subnets.

**ALBs** operate at HTTP Layer 7 (path-based, host-based, header-based routing; TLS termination; Cognito auth); **NLBs** at TCP/UDP Layer 4 (ultra-low latency, static IPs, non-HTTP protocols). Security groups are stateful instance-level firewalls; NACLs are stateless subnet-level firewalls — prefer security groups for most access control.

quiz.question: Which storage type should you use for a PostgreSQL database running on a cloud VM, and why?
options: Object storage (S3) — cheapest per GB and massively durable
Block storage (EBS gp3) — low-latency random IOPS required for database random read/write patterns
File storage (EFS) — shared across all database replicas simultaneously
Local instance store — fastest NVMe, best for all database workloads
quiz.explanation: Databases perform thousands of random reads and writes per second, requiring sub-millisecond latency. Block storage (EBS) behaves like a physical disk with predictable IOPS. Object storage has 5–50ms per-request latency — catastrophic for database I/O. Local instance store is fast but ephemeral (data lost on stop/terminate) and not suitable for production databases.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental technical difference between containers and virtual machines?
options: Containers run a full guest OS; VMs share the host kernel
VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor; containers share the host OS kernel via namespaces and cgroups
Containers are only used for stateless workloads; VMs always include persistent storage
VMs start in milliseconds; containers take minutes because they include more dependencies
quiz.explanation: VMs virtualize hardware and run a complete guest OS (kernel included) on top of a hypervisor. Containers share the host OS kernel, using Linux namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits. This makes containers lighter (~millisecond startup) but with shallower isolation than VMs.

quiz.question: An application needs to serve 50 TB of user-uploaded images globally with low cost. Which architecture is most appropriate?
options: EBS gp3 volumes attached to EC2 instances in each region
EFS shared filesystem mounted by web servers in each AZ
S3 object storage with CloudFront CDN for global edge caching
An in-memory Redis cluster for maximum throughput
quiz.explanation: S3 at ~$0.023/GB-month is 3.5x cheaper than EBS and 13x cheaper than EFS for the same data volume. Combined with CloudFront CDN, images are cached at edge locations near users globally. EBS cannot be accessed by multiple instances simultaneously (single-attach). Redis is an in-memory cache unsuitable for 50 TB of durable storage.

quiz.question: You need to move an EBS volume from us-east-1a to us-east-1b. What is the correct approach?
options: Detach from the instance in 1a and attach directly to an instance in 1b — EBS is regional
Create an EBS snapshot of the volume, then restore it as a new volume in us-east-1b
Enable EBS Multi-AZ replication in the volume settings
Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy the EBS data to 1b
quiz.explanation: EBS volumes are zone-scoped — a volume in us-east-1a physically resides in that AZ and cannot be directly attached to an instance in us-east-1b. The correct process is: create a snapshot (stored durably in S3), then create a new volume from the snapshot in the target AZ. EBS does not have a built-in Multi-AZ replication feature.

quiz.question: What is the critical difference between a public subnet and a private subnet in a VPC?
options: Private subnets use IPv6; public subnets use IPv4
Public subnets have a route to an Internet Gateway, allowing inbound internet traffic; private subnets do not
Private subnets are cheaper because they do not use an internet gateway
Public subnets are only for load balancers; private subnets are only for databases
quiz.explanation: The distinction is purely routing: a public subnet has a route table entry sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, allowing instances to receive inbound internet traffic (if they also have a public IP). Private subnets lack this route, so instances cannot receive unsolicited inbound internet traffic regardless of security group configuration — defense in depth.

quiz.question: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at OSI Layer 7. What routing capability does this enable that a Network Load Balancer (Layer 4) cannot provide?
options: Distributing traffic across multiple EC2 instances
Performing health checks on target instances
Routing based on HTTP URL path, hostname, or headers — for example /api/* to a backend service
Terminating TLS and decrypting HTTPS traffic
quiz.explanation: ALBs inspect decrypted HTTP content (Layer 7) and can route based on URL path (/api/* → backend microservice, /* → frontend SPA), hostname (api.example.com vs admin.example.com), or request headers. NLBs operate at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and route only based on IP and port — they cannot inspect HTTP content. Both can perform health checks and terminate TLS.

quiz.question: A security group rule on your database allows port 5432 from source sg-app (the application server security group). A new application server instance is launched and added to sg-app. Can this new instance reach the database?
options: No — the security group rule caches the instance IPs at rule creation time
Yes — security group source references are dynamic and automatically include all instances in the referenced group
Only if the new instance is in the same Availability Zone as the database
Yes, but only after the security group rule is manually refreshed
quiz.explanation: When a security group is referenced as a source, the rule dynamically applies to all instances currently associated with that security group — including newly launched instances. This is the key advantage of group-to-group rules over CIDR-based rules: no IP management required as the fleet scales.

quiz.question: Why is EFS (Elastic File System) approximately 13x more expensive per GB than S3 Standard?
options: EFS stores data in multiple regions simultaneously for global access
EFS provides POSIX-compatible shared filesystem semantics with synchronous consistency, requiring more complex distributed storage infrastructure
EFS automatically encrypts all data at rest with dedicated hardware security modules
EFS uses faster NVMe hardware than S3
quiz.explanation: EFS must maintain POSIX semantics (atomic rename, file locking, synchronous consistency) across a distributed NFS system mountable by hundreds of instances simultaneously. This requires significantly more complex infrastructure than S3's eventually-consistent key-value store model. The added complexity — not hardware differences — drives the price premium. S3 ~$0.023/GB-month; EFS ~$0.30/GB-month.

quiz.question: What is the key architectural reason to always place an ALB in at least two public subnets across different Availability Zones?
options: ALBs require two subnets to distribute SSL certificate processing load
AWS billing is cheaper with multi-AZ ALB configurations
If one AZ experiences an outage, the ALB nodes in the surviving AZs continue serving traffic, providing high availability
Security groups can only be attached to multi-AZ load balancers
quiz.explanation: An ALB deploys load balancer nodes in each specified AZ. If an AZ fails (power, networking, hardware), the nodes in other AZs take over automatically. A single-AZ ALB is a single point of failure — if that AZ has an outage, the entire application goes down. Multi-AZ deployment is a fundamental high availability requirement.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between Security Groups and Network ACLs (NACLs) in a VPC?
options: Security groups apply to subnets; NACLs apply to individual instances
Security groups are stateful (return traffic auto-allowed) and instance-scoped; NACLs are stateless (must explicitly allow both directions) and subnet-scoped
NACLs support security group references as sources; security groups only support CIDR blocks
Security groups evaluate all rules simultaneously; NACLs only evaluate the first matching rule and require numbered priorities
quiz.explanation: Security groups are stateful: an allowed inbound connection automatically permits the corresponding outbound response without an explicit rule. NACLs are stateless: you must create separate inbound and outbound rules for each allowed traffic flow, including ephemeral port ranges for responses. Security groups attach to instances/ENIs; NACLs attach to subnets and affect all resources in the subnet. Note: NACLs do evaluate rules in order and stop at the first match — but this is a secondary detail; the stateful vs stateless distinction is the primary difference.
